6.1 — Why milk is processed
Theory
Understand the idea

Raw milk is milk collected from dairy cattle before processing. After collection, it moves through a carefully managed pathway that helps prepare it for consumers. Processing is not one single step. It is a series of controlled stages, with each stage having a different purpose.

One important stage is pasteurisation. Pasteurisation is a controlled heat treatment that reduces disease-causing microorganisms that may be present in raw milk. This helps improve food safety before the milk continues through the production and distribution system. Pasteurisation should not be confused with other processing steps because its main purpose is to reduce harmful microorganisms.

Another stage is homogenisation. Homogenisation reduces the size of fat droplets so they remain more evenly distributed throughout the milk instead of separating into a distinct cream layer as quickly. This changes the physical appearance and consistency of the milk, but it is not the step that makes milk microbiologically safer. That purpose belongs to pasteurisation.

After processing, milk is packaged to help protect the product during storage, transport and sale. Packaging also provides important product information such as the product name and storage directions. Once packaged, milk is distributed through a refrigerated supply chain so suitable conditions are maintained while it travels to shops and other outlets.

A simple farm-to-consumer sequence is: milk is collected from dairy cattle, transported for processing, pasteurised, homogenised where required, packaged, distributed under refrigeration and purchased by consumers. Different dairy products may follow different pathways, but each stage has a specific role within the overall system.

Process controls are important because each stage must be carried out in a controlled way to support product quality, consistency and food safety. Students should be able to explain the purpose of each processing step rather than treating all stages as doing the same job. General claims about exact processing temperatures, times or shelf life require current product-specific information and should not be assumed from this overview.

Key takeaways

Raw milk is collected before processing and then moves through a controlled production pathway.

Pasteurisation uses controlled heat to reduce disease-causing microorganisms.

Homogenisation reduces fat-droplet size to keep milk more evenly mixed and does not make milk microbiologically safe.

Packaging and refrigerated distribution help protect processed milk as it moves to consumers.

Knowledge check

What is raw milk?
A. Milk collected before processing
B. Milk that has already been pasteurised
C. Milk that has already been packaged
D. Milk after refrigerated distribution

Answer: A. Milk collected before processing
Correct feedback: Correct. Raw milk is milk collected from dairy cattle before processing begins.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the opening sentence, which defines raw milk.
Source: Authorised Module 6 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1WbZxKJoZ-R1Sk7zBsKZkN6fokcFb4rHJguECuccWB-Q/edit; Food Standards Australia New Zealand — Raw drinking milk: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/Raw-drinking-milk; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing

What is the main purpose of pasteurisation?
A. To reduce disease-causing microorganisms using controlled heat
B. To keep fat evenly mixed through the milk
C. To package milk for transport
D. To change the flavour of milk

Answer: A. To reduce disease-causing microorganisms using controlled heat
Correct feedback: Correct. Pasteurisation uses controlled heat to reduce disease-causing microorganisms.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Focus on the specific purpose described in the second paragraph.
Source: Authorised Module 6 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1WbZxKJoZ-R1Sk7zBsKZkN6fokcFb4rHJguECuccWB-Q/edit; Food Standards Australia New Zealand — Raw drinking milk: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/Raw-drinking-milk; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing

What does homogenisation do?
A. Reduces the size of fat droplets so milk stays more evenly mixed
B. Reduces disease-causing microorganisms
C. Replaces refrigerated transport
D. Packages the milk for sale

Answer: A. Reduces the size of fat droplets so milk stays more evenly mixed
Correct feedback: Correct. Homogenisation changes the distribution of fat within the milk.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the paragraph explaining what happens to fat droplets during homogenisation.
Source: Authorised Module 6 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1WbZxKJoZ-R1Sk7zBsKZkN6fokcFb4rHJguECuccWB-Q/edit; Food Standards Australia New Zealand — Raw drinking milk: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/Raw-drinking-milk; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing

Which statement about homogenisation is correct?
A. It does not make milk microbiologically safe
B. It replaces pasteurisation
C. It removes all microorganisms from milk
D. It is the same process as packaging

Answer: A. It does not make milk microbiologically safe
Correct feedback: Correct. Homogenisation affects fat distribution, not microbiological safety.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. The theory clearly distinguishes homogenisation from pasteurisation.
Source: Authorised Module 6 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1WbZxKJoZ-R1Sk7zBsKZkN6fokcFb4rHJguECuccWB-Q/edit; Food Standards Australia New Zealand — Raw drinking milk: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/Raw-drinking-milk; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing

Why is milk packaged after processing?
A. To help protect the product during storage, transport and sale
B. To reduce disease-causing microorganisms
C. To replace refrigeration
D. To separate the fat from the milk

Answer: A. To help protect the product during storage, transport and sale
Correct feedback: Correct. Packaging helps protect the processed product through the supply chain.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Look at the paragraph explaining the role of packaging.
Source: Authorised Module 6 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1WbZxKJoZ-R1Sk7zBsKZkN6fokcFb4rHJguECuccWB-Q/edit; Food Standards Australia New Zealand — Raw drinking milk: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/Raw-drinking-milk; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing

Why is refrigerated distribution used?
A. To maintain suitable conditions while milk travels to consumers
B. To homogenise the milk
C. To pasteurise the milk again
D. To replace quality controls

Answer: A. To maintain suitable conditions while milk travels to consumers
Correct feedback: Correct. Refrigerated distribution helps maintain suitable conditions after processing.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the paragraph describing what happens after packaging.
Source: Authorised Module 6 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1WbZxKJoZ-R1Sk7zBsKZkN6fokcFb4rHJguECuccWB-Q/edit; Food Standards Australia New Zealand — Raw drinking milk: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/Raw-drinking-milk; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing

Which sequence best matches the farm-to-consumer pathway described?
A. Collection, processing, packaging, refrigerated distribution, consumer
B. Packaging, collection, pasteurisation, consumer, transport
C. Homogenisation, collection, packaging, consumer, processing
D. Consumer, packaging, processing, collection, transport

Answer: A. Collection, processing, packaging, refrigerated distribution, consumer
Correct feedback: Correct. This sequence follows the pathway described in the theory.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Read the farm-to-consumer sequence listed in the fifth paragraph.
Source: Authorised Module 6 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1WbZxKJoZ-R1Sk7zBsKZkN6fokcFb4rHJguECuccWB-Q/edit; Food Standards Australia New Zealand — Raw drinking milk: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/Raw-drinking-milk; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing

Why are process controls important?
A. They support product quality, consistency and food safety
B. They remove the need for packaging
C. They make every dairy product identical
D. They eliminate the need for refrigeration

Answer: A. They support product quality, consistency and food safety
Correct feedback: Correct. Process controls help support consistent quality and food safety.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the final paragraph about the purpose of process controls.
Source: Authorised Module 6 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1WbZxKJoZ-R1Sk7zBsKZkN6fokcFb4rHJguECuccWB-Q/edit; Food Standards Australia New Zealand — Raw drinking milk: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/Raw-drinking-milk; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing

Which processing step is mainly responsible for reducing disease-causing microorganisms?
A. Pasteurisation
B. Homogenisation
C. Packaging
D. Refrigerated distribution

Answer: A. Pasteurisation
Correct feedback: Correct. Pasteurisation is the controlled heat treatment that reduces disease-causing microorganisms.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Think about which step uses controlled heat for food safety.
Source: Authorised Module 6 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1WbZxKJoZ-R1Sk7zBsKZkN6fokcFb4rHJguECuccWB-Q/edit; Food Standards Australia New Zealand — Raw drinking milk: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/Raw-drinking-milk; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing

Why should students avoid assuming exact temperatures or processing times from this overview?
A. They require current product-specific information
B. Every dairy product uses identical conditions
C. Processing details never change
D. Temperatures are not part of dairy processing

Answer: A. They require current product-specific information
Correct feedback: Correct. Exact operating details depend on current product-specific information.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Read the final sentence explaining why exact figures are not included.
Source: Authorised Module 6 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1WbZxKJoZ-R1Sk7zBsKZkN6fokcFb4rHJguECuccWB-Q/edit; Food Standards Australia New Zealand — Raw drinking milk: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/Raw-drinking-milk; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing

Written evidence

Prompt: Explain the purpose of pasteurisation, homogenisation, packaging and refrigerated distribution in the farm-to-consumer milk pathway.
Scaffold:

Identify the relevant ideas and evidence from this section.

Explain the relationship clearly, using a specific example and respecting the source boundary.

Appropriate response example: Pasteurisation uses controlled heat to reduce disease-causing microorganisms. Homogenisation reduces the size of fat droplets so the milk stays more evenly mixed but does not make it microbiologically safe. Packaging protects the processed milk during storage and transport, while refrigerated distribution helps maintain suitable conditions until the product reaches consumers.
Source: Authorised Module 6 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1WbZxKJoZ-R1Sk7zBsKZkN6fokcFb4rHJguECuccWB-Q/edit; Food Standards Australia New Zealand — Raw drinking milk: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/Raw-drinking-milk; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing

Prompt: Trace the pathway from raw milk to the consumer and explain why process controls are important.
Scaffold:

Identify the relevant ideas and evidence from this section.

Explain the relationship clearly, using a specific example and respecting the source boundary.

Appropriate response example: Raw milk is collected from dairy cattle and transported for processing. It is pasteurised, homogenised where required, packaged and then distributed under refrigeration before being purchased by consumers. Process controls are important because each stage has a different purpose that supports product quality, consistency and food safety.
Source: Authorised Module 6 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1WbZxKJoZ-R1Sk7zBsKZkN6fokcFb4rHJguECuccWB-Q/edit; Food Standards Australia New Zealand — Raw drinking milk: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/Raw-drinking-milk; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing

Source boundary

Teach  the purpose of raw milk processing, pasteurisation, homogenisation, packaging and refrigerated distribution as separate stages within a controlled pathway. Do not include exact processing temperatures, processing times, shelf-life figures, local processing instructions or product-specific operating procedures.

sections.content:

6.2 — Food safety controls from farm to fridge
Theory
Understand the idea

Food safety from farm to fridge depends on a chain of control points rather than one final check. A control point is a stage where a hazard can be prevented, reduced or detected. A hazard is something that could make food unsafe, such as harmful microorganisms, contamination or loss of suitable storage conditions.

The first control point is collection and transport. Milk must move through a managed system that protects it from contamination and maintains suitable conditions before processing. Pasteurisation, or another approved equivalent process, is then used to reduce disease-causing microorganisms. This processing step does not remove the need for later controls.

After processing, recontamination must be avoided. Equipment, contact surfaces and handling systems must remain controlled so harmful material is not reintroduced. Sealed packaging provides another barrier by protecting the product during storage, transport and sale.

Temperature-controlled distribution helps maintain suitable conditions as milk moves through processing, transport, retail storage and the consumer’s fridge. A failure at one point can affect later stages, so the whole pathway must remain connected.

Traceability allows a product or batch to be followed through the supply chain. Records can show where milk came from, how it moved through processing and where it was distributed. Traceability supports investigation and response when a problem is identified.

For each control point, students can identify four elements: the hazard, the control used to manage it, the monitoring used to check the control, and the evidence showing that the check occurred. Evidence may include records, verified labels, sealed packaging or documented checks.

A product that looks, smells or appears normal is not proof that every food-safety control was followed. Appearance is only an observation. Reliable judgement requires evidence from the controlled process. Students must not handle or taste raw milk, apply operational settings or follow local procedures unless these are specifically authorised and supervised.

Key takeaways

Food safety depends on connected control points from collection to refrigerated storage.

Each control point can be examined through hazard, control, monitoring and evidence.

Sealed packaging and avoiding recontamination remain important after processing.

Normal appearance does not prove that food-safety controls were followed.

Knowledge check

What is a food-safety hazard?
A. Something that could make food unsafe
B. A record showing a control was completed
C. A sealed package ready for sale
D. A label naming the product

Answer: A. Something that could make food unsafe
Correct feedback: Correct. A hazard is something that could cause food to become unsafe.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the opening paragraph and distinguish a possible source of harm from evidence or packaging.
Source: Authorised Module 6 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1WbZxKJoZ-R1Sk7zBsKZkN6fokcFb4rHJguECuccWB-Q/edit; Food Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Raw drinking milk: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/Raw-drinking-milk

What is a control point?
A. A stage where a hazard can be prevented, reduced or detected
B. The final appearance of a dairy product
C. A marketing claim on packaging
D. A place where records are discarded

Answer: A. A stage where a hazard can be prevented, reduced or detected
Correct feedback: Correct. A control point is a stage where action can manage a food-safety hazard.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Focus on the stage in the pathway where a hazard can be controlled or detected.
Source: Authorised Module 6 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1WbZxKJoZ-R1Sk7zBsKZkN6fokcFb4rHJguECuccWB-Q/edit; Food Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Raw drinking milk: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/Raw-drinking-milk

What is the purpose of pasteurisation or an approved equivalent process?
A. To reduce disease-causing microorganisms
B. To seal the final package
C. To create traceability records
D. To prove the product looks acceptable

Answer: A. To reduce disease-causing microorganisms
Correct feedback: Correct. Pasteurisation or equivalent processing reduces disease-causing microorganisms.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the paragraph describing the main food-safety purpose of processing.
Source: Authorised Module 6 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1WbZxKJoZ-R1Sk7zBsKZkN6fokcFb4rHJguECuccWB-Q/edit; Food Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Raw drinking milk: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/Raw-drinking-milk

Why must recontamination be avoided after processing?
A. Harmful material could be introduced again
B. Processing makes later controls unnecessary
C. Packaging automatically removes all hazards
D. Refrigeration replaces clean handling systems

Answer: A. Harmful material could be introduced again
Correct feedback: Correct. Food can become contaminated again if later equipment or handling is not controlled.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Think about what could happen after microorganisms have already been reduced.
Source: Authorised Module 6 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1WbZxKJoZ-R1Sk7zBsKZkN6fokcFb4rHJguECuccWB-Q/edit; Food Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Raw drinking milk: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/Raw-drinking-milk

What is one purpose of sealed packaging?
A. To protect the product during storage and distribution
B. To pasteurise the milk
C. To replace traceability
D. To prove exact storage conditions were maintained

Answer: A. To protect the product during storage and distribution
Correct feedback: Correct. Sealed packaging provides a protective barrier after processing.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the paragraph explaining the barrier provided by packaging.
Source: Authorised Module 6 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1WbZxKJoZ-R1Sk7zBsKZkN6fokcFb4rHJguECuccWB-Q/edit; Food Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Raw drinking milk: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/Raw-drinking-milk

Why is temperature-controlled distribution important?
A. It helps maintain suitable conditions through the supply chain
B. It identifies the breed of dairy cattle
C. It removes the need for processing
D. It guarantees that no control can fail

Answer: A. It helps maintain suitable conditions through the supply chain
Correct feedback: Correct. Controlled distribution helps maintain suitable conditions from processing to refrigeration.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Focus on maintaining the product’s conditions as it moves between stages.
Source: Authorised Module 6 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1WbZxKJoZ-R1Sk7zBsKZkN6fokcFb4rHJguECuccWB-Q/edit; Food Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Raw drinking milk: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/Raw-drinking-milk

What does traceability allow?
A. A product or batch to be followed through the supply chain
B. A product’s safety to be judged from appearance
C. Operational settings to be invented by students
D. Packaging to replace all processing records

Answer: A. A product or batch to be followed through the supply chain
Correct feedback: Correct. Traceability links a product or batch with its movement through the supply chain.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the paragraph explaining how records support investigation and response.
Source: Authorised Module 6 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1WbZxKJoZ-R1Sk7zBsKZkN6fokcFb4rHJguECuccWB-Q/edit; Food Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Raw drinking milk: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/Raw-drinking-milk

Which item is evidence that a control was monitored?
A. A documented check
B. The product’s colour alone
C. A student’s guess
D. An unsupported claim

Answer: A. A documented check
Correct feedback: Correct. A documented check provides evidence that monitoring occurred.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Choose the option that records or verifies that the control was checked.
Source: Authorised Module 6 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1WbZxKJoZ-R1Sk7zBsKZkN6fokcFb4rHJguECuccWB-Q/edit; Food Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Raw drinking milk: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/Raw-drinking-milk

Why is normal appearance not enough to prove food safety?
A. Some control failures cannot be confirmed by appearance
B. Safe products must always look different
C. Packaging colour proves processing quality
D. Microorganisms are always clearly visible

Answer: A. Some control failures cannot be confirmed by appearance
Correct feedback: Correct. Appearance alone cannot confirm that each required control was followed.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the final paragraph and separate observation from process evidence.
Source: Authorised Module 6 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1WbZxKJoZ-R1Sk7zBsKZkN6fokcFb4rHJguECuccWB-Q/edit; Food Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Raw drinking milk: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/Raw-drinking-milk

What should students do when studying raw milk safety?
A. Analyse controls conceptually without handling or tasting raw milk
B. Test raw milk without supervision
C. Invent processing settings
D. Follow unconfirmed local procedures

Answer: A. Analyse controls conceptually without handling or tasting raw milk
Correct feedback: Correct. Students should study the control system without unauthorised handling or operational action.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. The theory sets a clear boundary against handling, tasting or applying unapproved procedures.
Source: Authorised Module 6 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1WbZxKJoZ-R1Sk7zBsKZkN6fokcFb4rHJguECuccWB-Q/edit; Food Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Raw drinking milk: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/Raw-drinking-milk

Written evidence

Prompt: Choose one control point from the farm-to-fridge pathway and identify its hazard, control, monitoring and evidence.
Scaffold:

Identify the relevant ideas and evidence from this section.

Explain the relationship clearly, using a specific example and respecting the source boundary.

Appropriate response example: At the packaging control point, the hazard is recontamination after processing. The control is sealed packaging. Monitoring checks whether packages are correctly closed and undamaged. Evidence could include documented packaging checks and inspection records.
Source: Authorised Module 6 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1WbZxKJoZ-R1Sk7zBsKZkN6fokcFb4rHJguECuccWB-Q/edit; Food Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Raw drinking milk: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/Raw-drinking-milk

Prompt: Explain why a dairy product’s appearance cannot prove that all food-safety controls were followed.
Scaffold:

Identify the relevant ideas and evidence from this section.

Explain the relationship clearly, using a specific example and respecting the source boundary.

Appropriate response example: A product may look and smell normal even if a control failed earlier in the pathway. Appearance is only an observation and cannot confirm pasteurisation, temperature control, packaging integrity or traceability. Reliable judgement requires records and other evidence showing that controls were monitored.
Source: Authorised Module 6 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1WbZxKJoZ-R1Sk7zBsKZkN6fokcFb4rHJguECuccWB-Q/edit; Food Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Raw drinking milk: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/prevention-of-foodborne-illness/Raw-drinking-milk

Teach  food-safety control points through hazard, control, monitoring and evidence. Do not provide operational settings, local procedures, handling instructions or permission for students to collect, taste or otherwise handle raw milk.

6.3 — Nutrition information and informed choice
Theory
Understand the idea

Milk, yoghurt, cheese and dairy alternatives can differ in ingredients, nutrients, allergens, processing and intended use. An informed choice uses product-specific evidence rather than assuming that one food is always healthier than another.

The ingredient list shows what has been used to make a product, usually arranged from the greatest to the smallest amount by weight. It can help consumers compare products with different ingredients, flavours, sweeteners or added nutrients. The nutrition information panel provides measured information about the product, such as energy, protein, fat, carbohydrate, sugars and sodium. Comparisons should use equivalent serving or quantity information shown on the labels.

The allergen statement identifies ingredients that may cause allergic reactions. Milk is an allergen, and some alternatives may contain other allergens. A label can support a general comparison, but students should not diagnose allergies or intolerance. Advice for a specific allergy, intolerance, health condition or medical diet must come from a qualified adult or health professional.

The Australian Dietary Guidelines provide a wider context for healthy eating. They encourage people to consider overall dietary patterns rather than judging one product in isolation. Nutritional needs can vary with age, life stage, activity and individual circumstances, so the same choice may not suit everyone.

Processing can change a product’s texture, flavour, ingredients, nutrient profile and shelf life. Milk may be processed into yoghurt or cheese, while alternatives may be made from plant ingredients and fortified with selected nutrients. However, broad product names do not reveal every property. The ingredient list, nutrition information panel, allergen statement and storage information provide the most relevant evidence for the specific packaged product.

A defensible comparison identifies the feature being compared, uses the same label information for each product and avoids unsupported health or disease-prevention claims. It should also acknowledge when personal medical guidance is required.

Key takeaways

Product labels provide specific evidence about ingredients, nutrients, allergens and storage.

Fair comparisons use the same nutrition information for each product.

Dietary needs vary with age, life stage, activity and individual circumstances.

Personal allergy, intolerance or medical nutrition advice must come from a qualified adult or health professional.

Knowledge check

What does an ingredient list show?
A. The ingredients used to make the product
B. A guaranteed health outcome
C. The consumer's personal dietary needs
D. A ranking of all similar foods

Answer: A. The ingredients used to make the product
Correct feedback: Correct. The ingredient list identifies what has been used to make the product.

Written evidence

Prompt: Compare two packaged milk, yoghurt, cheese or alternative products using the ingredient list, nutrition information panel and allergen statement.
Scaffold:

Identify the relevant ideas and evidence from this section.

Explain the relationship clearly, using a specific example and respecting the source boundary.

Appropriate response example: Product A lists milk as its main ingredient and identifies milk as an allergen. Product B uses plant ingredients and lists a different allergen. Using equivalent label quantities, Product A has more protein while Product B has less saturated fat. This comparison describes label evidence only and does not prove that either product is always healthier.

Source boundary

Teach  students to compare product-specific label evidence within a general dietary-guideline context. Do not prescribe servings, diagnose allergies or intolerance, provide personal medical nutrition advice, rank one product as universally healthier or make disease-prevention claims.
